newsitem.title: CANADA: Unharvested grain skews Canada grain stocks impact.
newsitem.headline: Unharvested grain skews Canada grain stocks impact.

text.p: Statistics Canada's grain and oilseed stocks report due Tuesday was expected to show lower supplies than February's report, but questions on how much of last fall's unharvested crop can still be salvaged had analysts dismissing the survey.
"Everyone's expecting low stocks numbers," Continental Grain analyst Greg Kostal said. "People will use the stocks report as a benchmark and twist it to whatever they want it to mean."
Three million acres of wheat, barley, canola, oats, flax and rye were not harvested on the western Prairies last fall due to early snowfall, provincial agriculture departments said.
Statistics Canada's March 31 stocks report is due May 13 at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
StatsCan's February 3 survey of on-farm stocks as of December 31 put all wheat stocks at 19.11 million tonnes, barley at 9.74 million tonnes and canola at 2.76 million tonnes.

"In the stocks report, it's just what's in the bin," Statistics Canada's head of grain marketing Karen Gray said. "If it's still in the field, it's not a stock. It doesn't become a stock until it's harvested."
The hardest hit region by the inclement fall weather was northern Alberta's Peace River Valley. More crops are likely to be salvaged in northern Saskatchewan, analysts said.

There were 307,234 acres of wheat, 225,703 acres of barley and 191,746 acres of canola in northern Alberta that was not harvested last fall. About two million acres of the six major crops were not harvested, Alberta Agriculture said.
Another 950,000 acres seeded to the six major crops in northern Saskatchewan were not harvested, Saskatchewan Agriculture said.
The amount of salvageable grains and oilseeds was a point of contention between analysts.

"We would suspect a maximum quantity of 200,000 tonnes of wheat will still be useable but probably less than that. The barley's written off and canola, maybe 20,000 tonnes," James Richardson International Ltd analyst David Champion said.
"The winter was so hard on it, so much snow, so much freeze and thaw, that stuff just got so chewed up it deteriorated. A lot of the canola shattered," Champion said.
United Grain Growers Ltd analyst Mike Jubinville said he expected all canola in northern Alberta to be unuseable and burned by farmers.
"I think 500,000 tonnes of barley, 800,000 to one million tonnes of wheat and 100,000 tonnes of canola will be lost," LFG vice president Rob Dzisiak said. "I think most of the flax will be okay."
